notes: Customs condemnation extension-of-time judicial review; unlawful discretion framework and outcome are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Customs judicial review of out-of-time condemnation appeals
key_facts: Customs and Excise applied for judicial review of HHJ Simpson's grants of extensions of time to appeal condemnation orders in two Maidstone Crown Court cases.

Michael Graham failed to attend a Dover magistrates' condemnation hearing in January 2002; his application to appeal was made about 16 months later citing unawareness of the hearing and a road accident.
Gerald McSorley attended his condemnation hearing in May 2002 but did not lodge an appeal notice until November 2003, about 18 months later.
In each case tobacco, cigarettes, alcohol or a vehicle had been condemned after customs seizures.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Crown Court grants of extensions of time to appeal magistrates' condemnation orders.
enrichment.outcome: Judicial review applications succeeded; both grants of extension of time were quashed.
enrichment.ratio: A Crown Court judge exercising discretion under Crown Court Rule 7 to extend time for appeal must consider both the reasons for delay and the merits of the proposed appeal; where months of unexplained delay coincide with scant appeal merits and no adequate explanation, granting leave is an unlawful failure to address relevant considerations.
legal_issues: Framework for exercising discretion to extend time to appeal to the Crown Court
Whether reasons for delay and merits of appeal must both be considered
Whether affected parties should receive reasons when extensions of time are granted
Whether section 142 Magistrates' Courts Act applied to condemnation proceedings

notes: Licensing Act s169A corporate liability appeal; Pepper v Hart analysis and stated case answers are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Supermarket corporate liability for under-age alcohol sales
key_facts: Haringey and Liverpool local authorities prosecuted Marks & Spencer and Somerfield for selling alcohol to persons under 18.
Licences were held by named employee licensees, not the corporate supermarket operators.
District judges dismissed summonses on the basis the companies were not a person within section 169A of the Licensing Act 1964.
In the Somerfield case the individual seller pleaded guilty; in Marks & Spencer a due diligence defence would have succeeded even if corporate liability existed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeals by case stated from magistrates' court dismissals of prosecutions against corporate supermarket operators.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; corporate owner or employer not a person for section 169A(1); defendant's costs orders made; certification for leave to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Read in the context of the Licensing Act 1964, section 169A was intended only to extend liability to previously omitted employees of a licensee, not to corporate proprietors or employers who are not licence holders; giving a person different meanings in sections 160 and 169A would produce absurd results.
legal_issues: Whether a corporate supermarket operator is a person under section 169A(1)
Whether section 169A extends liability to non-licensed corporate proprietors
Use of Hansard under Pepper v Hart to construe the 2000 amendment
Relationship between due diligence defence and corporate prosecution

notes: Drug trafficking confiscation appeal; Benjafield injustice analysis and Crown concession handling are explicit.

enrichment.short_title: Confiscation order quashed after Crown trafficking concession
key_facts: Lunnon pleaded guilty to conspiring to supply cannabis after a large importation concealed in scrap metal from Holland to Sheffield.
He was sentenced to 13 months' imprisonment and later made subject to a confiscation order of £12,371.29 with an eight-month default sentence.
The Crown accepted he had no previous involvement in drug trafficking and had received no financial benefit from the conspiracy.
Judge Swanson applied statutory assumptions under section 4(3) without returning to the Crown's concession on prior trafficking.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by leave of the single judge against a confiscation order made following conviction for drug trafficking conspiracy.
enrichment.ratio: Where the Crown concedes a defendant had no prior drug trafficking involvement, the court must stand back under section 4(4)(b) and address whether applying statutory assumptions would risk serious injustice; ignoring an unwithdrawn concession without reasoned explanation renders a confiscation order unsafe.
legal_issues: Application of statutory assumptions under section 4(3) of the Drug Trafficking Act 1994
Effect of a Crown concession that a defendant had no prior drug trafficking
Obligation to avoid serious injustice under section 4(4)(b)
Compatibility of reverse burden with Article 6 following Benjafield
linked_authorities: R v Benjafield [2003] 1 AC 1099
R v Rezvi [2001] 3 WLR 75
R v Benjafield [2003] 1 AC 1161

confidence.notes: Outcome and statutory framework are clear; judge's failure to address the Crown concession is central and well documented.

notes: Landmark HIV transmission s20 appeal; Clarence erosion, consent analysis, and retrial order are fully reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Reckless HIV transmission and consent under section 20
key_facts: Mohammed Dica was convicted of two counts of inflicting grievous bodily harm under section 20 after consensual unprotected sex with two women while HIV positive.
He knew his HIV status from 1995 but did not deliberately seek to infect the complainants; recklessness was not disputed if section 20 applied.
The trial judge ruled Clarence was no longer authoritative and that complainants' consent to intercourse did not provide a defence.
Dica elected not to give evidence after those rulings and was sentenced to eight years' imprisonment in total.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with leave of the trial judge against conviction for section 20 offences; sentence referred to the full court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; convictions quashed; retrial ordered on consent and recklessness issues; sentence not addressed pending retrial.
enrichment.ratio: R v Clarence no longer governs section 20 liability for transmission of disease; concealment of HIV vitiates consent to the risk of infection, but knowing consent to that risk remains a defence, and Brown does not criminalise consensual intercourse where adults knowingly accept infection risk.
legal_issues: Whether reckless HIV transmission can constitute section 20 grievous bodily harm
Continuing authority of R v Clarence on sexually transmitted disease
Whether consent to sexual intercourse includes consent to risk of infection
Application of R v Brown to consensual sexual activity

R v Ireland; R v Burstow [1998] 1 CAR 177

notes: Implacable hostility contact appeal; transfer to Division, NYAS, and therapy directions are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Father's contact appeal and implacable hostility
key_facts: A father sought permission to appeal orders limiting contact with his children L, nearly 13, and A, about 10.
Contact had a long history of non-compliance; the mother did not attend the Court of Appeal hearing citing pregnancy complications.
HHJ Shipley had ordered only six-weekly three-hour visiting contact with A, which had not taken place.
The guardian and CAFCASS were criticised as insufficiently interventionist; the mother was said to be implacably opposed to contact.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Oral hearing on application for permission to appeal family contact orders, with appeal to follow if permission granted.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted; case transferred to a High Court Family Division judge for urgent hearing before July 2004; NYAS invited; family therapy urged; May and June contact visits ordered to proceed.
enrichment.ratio: Where years of litigation show implacable obstruction to contact and existing orders are ineffective, the court should elevate the case to a Family Division judge, enforce pending contact, and deploy therapeutic and advocacy resources before adolescence makes contact irrecoverable.
legal_issues: Whether the mother's conduct amounted to implacable hostility
Appropriate judicial level and urgency for intractable contact disputes
Role of CAFCASS versus NYAS in implementing contact orders
Whether family therapy should be pursued despite parental refusal
linked_authorities: A v A [2004] EWCA Civ 2
Wall LJ contact jurisprudence

confidence.notes: Procedural directions and reasoning are clear; underlying factual disputes about contact breaches remain contested.

notes: Planning floorspace appeal on pergola; inspector reasoning and Elias J dismissal are straightforward.

enrichment.short_title: Rural extension floorspace and pergola planning appeal
key_facts: Mr and Mrs Cannon sought planning permission for a pergola and gates at their Berkhamsted cottage.
Dacorum Borough Council refused the application; a planning inspector allowed the appeal on the papers in December 2003.
The dispute centred on Local Plan Policy 23 criterion requiring total floorspace to remain below 150% of the original dwelling.
The house was already at 254% before the proposal; the council argued the pergola added 13 square metres taking it to 276%.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 appeal against a planning inspector's decision allowing an appeal from refusal of planning permission.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; inspector's decision upheld; permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Whether space beneath an open-sided pergola constitutes floorspace under a local plan depends on the purpose and character of the structure; an essentially aesthetic shelter over gates need not be treated as additional floorspace merely because it could theoretically be used for storage.
legal_issues: Meaning of floorspace under Dacorum Local Plan Policy 23
Whether a pergola over driveway gates engages the 150% floorspace limit
Whether the inspector erred on gate opening direction or usability of space
Whether usable potential alone compels floorspace classification
linked_authorities: Edwards v Bairstow principles on inspector decisions

confidence.notes: Single issue on floorspace interpretation; inspector reasoning accepted as rational though not felicitously expressed.

notes: Mental health s117 deferred discharge case; Winterwerp, IH, and best endeavours analysis are detailed and clear.

enrichment.short_title: Deferred conditional discharge and section 117 after-care
key_facts: W, a restricted patient detained since 1994 for knife violence, was conditionally discharged by a tribunal in July 2001 subject to deferred conditions including approved accommodation.
Doncaster Council, as section 117 authority, could not secure agreed accommodation at Westfield House and explored alternatives over many months.
A second tribunal in March 2002 directed discharge to Westfield House; W remained detained between July 2001 and March 2002.
W claimed false imprisonment and Human Rights Act damages against the council for failing to implement the July tribunal order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against dismissal of claims for false imprisonment and Human Rights Act damages relating to delayed conditional discharge.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; council not in breach of section 117; no unlawful detention or Article 5 breach; reporting restrictions on appellant's name continued.
enrichment.ratio: Where a tribunal defers conditional discharge until approved accommodation and supervision are in place, continued detention is lawful if the section 117 authority uses best endeavours to implement the conditions; failure to secure a preferred placement amid genuine professional concerns does not amount to false imprisonment or Convention breach.
legal_issues: Lawfulness of detention pending implementation of deferred conditional discharge
Scope of section 117 after-care duty before and after tribunal discharge
Whether Winterwerp criteria were satisfied during the disputed period
Availability of damages against a section 117 authority for delayed discharge

notes: Large VAT carousel fraud judgment; ECJ reference on Article 28 is clear but domestic outcomes on assessments await EU ruling.

enrichment.short_title: Mobile phone VAT zero-rating and carousel fraud
key_facts: Wholesale mobile phone traders supplied phones ex works to Total Telecom Espana SA in Spain for delivery to France or Spain.
Phones were placed at Euro-Cellars warehouse; CMR transport documents were later shown to be false and phones allegedly never left the UK.
Customs assessed claimants to VAT after discovering fabricated carriers, destinations and vehicle details.
Claimants argued zero-rating was available once goods were placed at the purchaser's disposal for removal to another Member State.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Multiple linked applications for judicial review of VAT assessments and related customs decisions.
enrichment.outcome: Article 28 Sixth Directive interpretation referred to the European Court of Justice; claimants' initial enquiries held reasonable; CMR documents found false; section 30(10) and section 81(3) issues deferred pending ECJ ruling; judicial review held appropriate forum.
enrichment.ratio: Whether intra-Community supply exemption under Article 28 requires physical removal before zero-rating is a question for the ECJ; innocent traders who conducted reasonable enquiries cannot be faulted for inability to detect sophisticated false transport documents, but assessments may await the correct EU interpretation.
legal_issues: Whether Article 28 requires goods to leave the Member State before zero-rating
Conditions for exempt intra-Community supplies of goods
Whether assessments were an abuse of power against innocent traders
Whether judicial review was appropriate rather than tribunal appeals

notes: Camas takeover fees as s75 management expenses; Sun Life test application and appeal dismissal are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Takeover advisory fees as expenses of management
key_facts: Camas Plc, an investment company, incurred about £583,495 in professional fees evaluating a possible acquisition of Bardon Group Plc.
Advisers included Schroders, Warburgs, KPMG, Clifford Chance and US counsel on strategy, due diligence and offer documentation.
A conditional approach was made on 19 December 1995 and abandoned on 21 December when Bardon rejected it; no acquisition occurred.
Special Commissioners held the fees were part of projected acquisition costs not deductible as expenses of management.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Revenue appeal against High Court decision allowing deduction of takeover advisory fees under ICTA section 75(1).
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; fees deductible as expenses of management; capital expenditure exclusion argument rejected.
enrichment.ratio: Under the Sun Life test, professional fees for investigating and deciding whether to acquire a particular target are severable from the cost of acquisition and qualify as expenses of management; they remain managerial even if also a necessary prerequisite to mounting a bid.
legal_issues: Whether pre-acquisition advisory fees are expenses of management under section 75(1)
Application of the Sun Life severability test to aborted takeovers
Whether section 75 excludes capital expenditure
Treatment of dual-purpose due diligence and board decision costs

notes: BP CAR insurance construction issue; Colman J ruling on co-extensive contractor cover is detailed and definitive.

enrichment.short_title: Construction All Risks cover and waiver of subrogation
key_facts: BP claimed defective subsea control modules and valves supplied by Kvaerner caused loss exceeding £13.5 million on the Schiehallion field project.
BP's insurers pursued a subrogated claim limited to £7,076,976 paid under a Construction All Risks policy.
Kvaerner argued insurers had waived subrogation rights; Cooper Cameron was joined for contribution on valve contamination issues.
The preliminary issue was whether Development Contract clause 10.5(b) obliged BP to procure co-extensive CAR cover for contractors.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of preliminary issues on Construction All Risks insurance cover and waiver of subrogation against Kvaerner and Cooper Cameron.
enrichment.outcome: Kvaerner and Cooper Cameron entitled to co-extensive CAR cover as Other Assureds; clause 10.5(b) read as free-standing obligation not limited by opening words of clause 10.5.
enrichment.ratio: Despite layout suggesting otherwise, clause 10.5(b) of the Development Contract requires BP to procure Construction All Risks cover co-extensive with that available to BP for contractor performance; the Notes on Insurance and policy wording indicate mutual intention beyond post-delivery attendance only.
legal_issues: Construction of clause 10.5(b) insurance obligation in offshore development contract
Whether contractor cover is limited to post-delivery installation and remedial attendance
